To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the current approaches to privacy are not sufficient to prevent sensitive behaviors from being inferred from sensor data; (b) there is an opportunity to improve user privacy by taking into account context information, such as location, and by using it to reduce the sensitivity of data; and (c) the tradeoff between utility and privacy is best addressed using a framework for privacy that is context-aware.

we present a novel framework for context-aware sharing of personal sensor data on mobile devices that allows the user to control the level of privacy and the level of utility, and that we demonstrate the effectiveness and feasibility of the framework with a prototype system and a set of experiments.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the user should be able to control how much of her sensor data is shared with an app, and how much privacy is provided.

the privacy of sensor data can be preserved by using a combination of two techniques: (i) a context-aware anonymization mechanism that uses contextual information about the user's current environment to hide the sensitive behaviors; and (ii) a privacy-preserving mechanism that prevents the app producer from linking the anonymized data back to the user.
the utility of sharing sensor data can be increased by sharing only a subset of the data, and that this subset should be chosen carefully, so that the privacy of the user is preserved.
